chapters.title: The Gettysburg Address (November 19, 1863)
paragraphs: Eighty-seven years ago, our fathers created on this continent a new nation, born in liberty and committed to the idea that all men are created equal.

Today we are fighting a great civil war… a test of whether that nation, or any nation born this way and committed to these ideals… can last for long. We have gathered on a great battlefield of that war.
We have come to set aside part of this field as a final resting place for those who gave their lives here so that this nation might live. It is entirely right and proper for us to do this.

But in a deeper sense, we cannot dedicate… we cannot consecrate… we cannot make holy this ground. The brave men, living and dead, who fought here have already made it sacred, far beyond anything our weak powers can add or take away. The world will pay little attention to what we say here, and will not remember it for long, but it can never forget what they did here.

Instead, it is for us, the living, to dedicate ourselves here to the unfinished work that those who fought here have carried so nobly forward. It is for us to dedicate ourselves to the great task that still lies before us… that from these honored dead we draw greater devotion to the cause for which they gave the last full measure of devotion… that we here firmly resolve that these dead will not have died in vain… that this nation, under God, will have a new birth of freedom… and that government of the people… by the people… for the people… will not vanish from the earth.

chapters.title: The Second Inaugural Address (March 4, 1865)
paragraphs: Fellow countrymen: Now that I am taking the oath of the presidential office a second time, there is less reason for a long speech than there was the first time. Then it seemed right to lay out in some detail the course I would follow. Now, four years later, public statements have been made constantly on every point and stage of this great struggle, which still holds the attention and absorbs the energies of the nation, and there is little new to offer. Our military progress, on which everything else mainly depends, is as well known to the public as it is to me, and I trust it is reasonably satisfying and encouraging to everyone. I have high hopes for the future, but I will not venture any prediction about it.

Four years ago, at this same occasion, everyone’s thoughts were anxiously fixed on a civil war that was about to begin. All dreaded it—all tried to prevent it. While the inaugural address was being given from this spot, aimed entirely at saving the Union without war, rebel agents were in the city, trying to destroy it without war—trying to break up the Union and divide its property through negotiation. Both sides disapproved of war; but one of them would make war rather than let the nation survive, and the other would accept war rather than let it die. And the war came.

One-eighth of the whole population were enslaved Black people, who were not spread across the Union but lived mainly in its southern part. These slaves made up a distinct and powerful interest. Everyone knew that this interest was somehow the cause of the war. Strengthening, prolonging, and expanding it was the goal for which the rebels would tear the Union apart, even by war; while the government claimed no right to do more than limit its spread into new territory.

Neither side expected the war to grow as large or last as long as it already has. Neither imagined that the cause of the conflict might end when the conflict ended, or even before. Each hoped for an easier victory and a result less fundamental and astounding. Both sides read the same Bible and pray to the same God, and each calls on him for help against the other. It may seem strange that any men would dare to ask a just God to help them wring their bread from the sweat of other men’s faces; but let us not judge, so that we will not be judged. The prayers of both could not be answered—neither has been answered fully.

The Almighty has his own purposes. “Woe to the world because of offenses! for it must needs be that offenses come; but woe to that man by whom the offense comes.” Suppose we take American slavery to be one of those offenses which, in God’s providence, had to come, but which he now wills to remove, since it has lasted through its appointed time; and suppose he gives this terrible war to both North and South as the woe due to those by whom the offense came. Would we then see any departure from the divine qualities that believers in a living God always attribute to him? We hope sincerely—we pray earnestly—that this mighty scourge of war will soon pass away. Yet if God wills that it continue until all the wealth the bondsman piled up through two hundred and fifty years of unpaid labor is lost, and until every drop of blood drawn by the lash is paid for by another drawn by the sword, then, as was said three thousand years ago, so it must still be said, “The judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether.”

Bearing malice toward no one, and charity toward all, and holding firm to the right as God lets us see the right, let us keep working to finish the task we are in; to heal the nation’s wounds; to look after the soldier who has fought the battle, and his widow, and his orphan—to do everything we can to win and treasure a just and lasting peace, among ourselves and with all nations.
